passage: "So are you coming to the trek or not?" Akash asked, tossing a cricket ball from hand to hand. Jahnavi pressed her lips together and raised one eyebrow. "Maybe." "Maybe yes or maybe no?" "Maybe I need to see who else is going." Her brother leaned on the doorframe. "Jahnavi, it's just three days." She looked at her feet. "Ma will ask about the river crossing. I don't know if I can say it isn't dangerous." Akash stopped tossing. "I hadn't thought of that. Okay, want to ask the teacher together?" She looked up. "Yes. That would help." He put the ball down and they went to find the permission form.

qa.q: How many days is the trek?
qa.a: Three days.

qa.q: What is Jahnavi feeling behind her maybe?
qa.a: She is unsure and a bit worried about the river crossing, and she does not want to promise her mother something she cannot check. Her raised eyebrow and looking down suggest careful thinking as well as fear.

qa.q: What did Akash do that helped?
qa.a: He stopped pushing, took in her worry, and offered to ask the teacher with her.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi's mother see the trek?
qa.a: She would probably focus on safety, especially the river crossing, so clear answers from the teacher would help her decide.

grounding: A teen hesitates and says maybe about a plan, and open discussion works better than pressure.

passage: When my uncle asked whether I would join the family business after school, I said, "Maybe," and raised my brow the way I do when I am not sure. I did not want to lie and I did not want to argue. Later, on the verandah, I told my mother I had doubts, not because I disliked the shop but because I was afraid I would be bad at it. She listened and did not correct me. My cousin Keerthana overheard and said, "I'm unsure too. About everything." We laughed a little. I felt lighter. Doubt is not the same as no. I think it means I am still thinking, and maybe a bit scared 🙂

qa.q: What did the narrator say when the uncle asked about the business?
qa.a: The narrator said, "Maybe," and raised a brow.

qa.q: What was the narrator feeling behind the doubt?
qa.a: The narrator was unsure and afraid of being bad at the work, not really disliking the shop. The doubt was both careful thinking and fear.

qa.q: What could the narrator do to think it through without pressure?
qa.a: The narrator could keep talking with the mother, try the work a little, and ask more questions before deciding.

qa.q: How might Keerthana's remark have helped?
qa.a: Hearing that Keerthana is unsure too likely made the narrator feel less alone, since it showed doubt is common.

grounding: A teen hesitates and says maybe, and the doubt reflects both thinking and fear, eased by open talk.

subtype: Reading interest and confusion in others [Interpreting]
passage: Room 12 was hot, the ceiling fan clicking as Mr. Iyer wrote the formula on the board. Pradeep, at the desk by the window, watched Chaitanya two rows ahead. Chaitanya's head tilted, his eyes narrowed at the board, and his pen stopped moving. Pradeep thought, He is lost. But Chaitanya also stared out of the window once, and that could be boredom. Pradeep leaned forward and whispered, "Did you get that last step?" Chaitanya turned, relieved. "No! I thought it was only me." "Want to ask him together?" Chaitanya put his hand up, half a second before Pradeep did, and Mr. Iyer smiled and started the step again.

qa.q: Where was Pradeep sitting?
qa.a: At the desk by the window.

qa.q: What made Pradeep think Chaitanya might be confused?
qa.a: Chaitanya's head tilted, his eyes narrowed and his pen stopped, but Pradeep also saw him stare out of the window, which could mean boredom. He treated the cues as hints and asked.

qa.q: What is a better choice than assuming a classmate's state?
qa.a: Ask quietly, as Pradeep did, because a face and voice only give hints.

qa.q: How did Chaitanya feel when Pradeep asked?
qa.a: He felt relieved that he was not the only one lost, and that someone had noticed.

grounding: A teen reads a classmate's interest, puzzlement or boredom as hints and asks to check.

subtype: Reading interest and confusion in others [Interpreting]
passage: Dear Suraj, I've been meaning to write since the science fair. During your presentation Naveen here was watching the girls in the front row, and honestly I thought half of them looked bored. One was yawning, one stared at the ceiling. I felt bad for you. But afterwards the same girl asked you three questions, and I was shocked. So the yawn meant nothing? Maybe she was just tired. Maybe the ceiling was her way of thinking. I decided I shouldn't judge from the faces. Next time I'll ask, "Did that make sense?" and see. Anyway, your project was great. Your friend, Naveen

qa.q: How many questions did the girl ask Suraj afterwards?
qa.a: Three questions.

qa.q: What did Naveen think when he saw the girls yawning and looking at the ceiling?
qa.a: He thought they looked bored and felt bad for Suraj, but the later questions showed the yawn did not mean disinterest. He concluded cues are hints only.

qa.q: What could Naveen do next time instead of guessing from faces?
qa.a: He could ask, "Did that make sense?" and listen to the answer.

qa.q: How might Suraj have felt during the presentation?
qa.a: He may have felt nervous when he saw a yawn, and encouraged when a girl asked questions later.

grounding: A teen tries to read interest, puzzlement or boredom from faces and learns they are only hints.

passage: The rain was hammering the tin roof of the internet café when the results page finally loaded. Gurleen leaned over the screen, and Nilesh, her cousin, stood behind. The noise of the rain made it hard to hear anything. She read her number, then read it again. Her mouth opened but no sound came out. She froze, her hand at her chest, eyes wide. "Gurleen?" Nilesh said. She didn't answer. He didn't tell her to say something; he waited. After a while, she whispered, "I got the scholarship." Then she began to laugh and cry at once, and Nilesh stood quietly until she was ready to leave the desk.

qa.q: Where were Gurleen and Nilesh when the results loaded?
qa.a: In an internet cafe with rain on the tin roof.

qa.q: What was Gurleen feeling when she froze at the screen?
qa.a: She was astonished, more than simply surprised, and it turned into joy, shown by her laughing and crying together. Freezing and staring can also come with distress, so only her whisper confirmed which.

qa.q: What did Nilesh do that helped?
qa.a: He gave her quiet space and waited without demanding an answer, which let her take in the news.

qa.q: How might Nilesh have felt while waiting?
qa.a: He may have felt anxious not knowing the news and relieved and proud when she whispered that she got the scholarship.

grounding: A teen freezes and stares at shocking news of results, and a moment of quiet space helps.

passage: "Joseph, look at this," Reena said, sliding into the seat beside him on the metro. She held out her phone with the message from the college. Joseph read it and gasped, one hand over his mouth. He froze. The train went through a tunnel and the lights flickered. Reena said nothing, just watched him. He read it a third time. "They picked my short film," he said slowly. "For the festival." She squealed, then lowered her voice. "Are you okay?" He nodded, eyes shining. "I don't know how I feel. It's big. Too big." She squeezed his sleeve gently. "Then sit. We have six stops." He sat, breathing, and started grinning.

qa.q: How many stops did they have left?
qa.a: Six stops.

qa.q: What was Joseph feeling when he read the message?
qa.a: He was astonished, a stronger state than surprise, and it slowly turned to joy, with shining eyes and a grin. He himself says it is too big to name yet.

qa.q: What did Reena do that helped Joseph?
qa.a: She gave him space, spoke softly and told him to sit, so he could take in the news at his own pace.

qa.q: How might Reena be feeling for Joseph?
qa.a: She is likely happy and excited for him, shown by her squeal, and a little careful not to overwhelm him.

grounding: A teen gasps and freezes at unexpected news, and quiet space helps the astonishment settle into joy.

subtype: Excited, eager and worried mixed together [Mismatch]
passage: Counsellor's note, Class 10. Yamini and her friend Vaibhav visited me before the interview trip. Yamini said her heart was racing and her stomach fluttering, and she was sure she was going to fail. Vaibhav said, "Mine is the same, and I can't tell if I'm scared or excited." I explained, without medical detail, that eager and nervous can feel much the same in the body, and that some people find it useful to call it excitement. Yamini tried saying, "I'm excited," and her shoulders dropped a little. I do not know whether this will last. I suggested a short walk before the interview. If the worry stays heavy, they can come back to me.

qa.q: What did Yamini say she felt in her body?
qa.a: Her heart was racing and her stomach was fluttering.

qa.q: What did Yamini and Vaibhav seem to be feeling before the trip?
qa.a: They seemed to feel both eager and nervous at once, and Vaibhav could not tell fear from excitement. The same racing heart can carry either.

qa.q: What did the counsellor suggest that might help?
qa.a: They suggested labelling the feeling as excitement and taking a short walk before the interview, with a return visit if the worry stayed heavy.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav have felt hearing that Yamini had the same feelings?
qa.a: He may have felt relieved to know he was not alone and that his racing heart was normal.

grounding: A teen before an interview feels eager and anxious at once, and labelling it as excitement helps turn nervous energy into readiness.

subtype: Excited, eager and worried mixed together [Mismatch]
passage: Monday night. Tomorrow is the first day of my job at the bakery and I can't stop pacing. My heart is thumping like I've run up stairs. My first thought was, I'm terrified, I'll burn everything. Then I remembered what my cousin Gurpreet said about racing hearts: sometimes it's just excitement wearing a scary mask. So I tried it out loud in the mirror: "I'm excited!" It felt a bit silly and a bit true. I still don't know the recipes and I still worry. But I could feel my hands relax and I laid out my apron. I'm going to sleep now (I hope) 😴 Madhuri

qa.q: What did Madhuri remember about racing hearts, and from whom?
qa.a: Her cousin Gurpreet said sometimes it's just excitement wearing a scary mask.

qa.q: How does Madhuri feel about starting the job?
qa.a: She feels both terrified and excited, and the same racing heart carries both. Calling it excitement helped her hands relax, though she still has worries.

qa.q: What could Madhuri do if the worry gets heavy tomorrow?
qa.a: She could take a breath, remind herself the feeling is nervous energy, and ask a coworker or supervisor for guidance.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet feel knowing the advice helped?
qa.a: Gurpreet would probably feel glad and encouraged that a small idea helped his cousin.

grounding: A teen before a first job feels eager and anxious together and turns nervous energy into readiness by labelling it excitement.

passage: With ten seconds left and the gym roaring, Kamal's shot dropped through the net. The buzzer howled. Kamal pumped both fists and ran to hug his teammates, sweat on every face. Rukmini, the other team's captain and his cousin, stood at half-court, jaw tight, staring at the floor. The crowd chanted his name. Kamal caught her eye and slowed, his grin dimming. He jogged over. "Great game," he said, and held out his hand. She shook it, rough at first, then more gently. "You too," she said. He didn't say anything about the score. Behind them the noise carried on, but he stayed a moment longer next to her.

qa.q: How many seconds were left when Kamal scored?
qa.a: Ten seconds.

qa.q: What was Kamal feeling after the shot, and how did that change?
qa.a: He felt triumphant, shown by the fist pumps and hugging, but he slowed when he saw Rukmini's tight jaw, so he began to think about her feelings too.

qa.q: What could Kamal do to share his win graciously?
qa.a: He could thank Rukmini for the game, avoid bragging and give her a moment before celebrating.

qa.q: How might Rukmini feel at half-court?
qa.a: She is probably disappointed and hurt, and Kamal's handshake may have softened that a little.

grounding: A teen cheers and hugs after a win, then shares the triumph graciously when the opponent hurts.

passage: Abhinav's hands were still shaking when the school relay team crossed the line first. He punched the air, screamed, and jumped into his teammates' arms while parents cheered from the stands. His friend Irfan, who had missed the team by one place in the trials, clapped from the fence. Abhinav ran over, flushed and glowing. He almost said, "Look how fast I was!" Then he saw Irfan's smile, a little stiff. So he said, "I wish you had been on the track with us." Irfan looked surprised, then grinned properly. "Next year." "Next year," Abhinav agreed, and they walked to the water stand together.

qa.q: Where did Irfan stand while clapping?
qa.a: At the fence.

qa.q: What was Abhinav feeling after the relay, and what did he decide about Irfan?
qa.a: He felt triumphant and proud, and he saw Irfan's stiff smile and held back the bragging, choosing kindness instead.

qa.q: What could Irfan do with his mixed feelings?
qa.a: He could admit to Abhinav that it stings and still cheer, and keep training for next year's trials.

qa.q: How might Irfan see Abhinav's words?
qa.a: He probably felt seen and included, because Abhinav did not gloat, and that eased the sting.

grounding: A teen celebrates a win and shares it graciously rather than gloating, noticing a friend's hurt.

passage: At the tea stall by the bus stand, Tushar leaned on the counter and said, without a flicker of expression, "Ganga, your hair looks like a crow's nest." Ganga turned slowly. His face was perfectly flat. The tea seller stopped pouring. Ganga kept her own face flat. "Thank you. I worked on it all morning." A pause. Then Tushar's mouth twitched, and Ganga burst into laughter. The tea seller shook his head. Later Ganga said, "Tushar, when you do that face, I can't tell if you're joking. Tell me sometimes, please." Tushar nodded. "Okay. Only when you look worried." She grinned.

qa.q: Where were Tushar and Ganga?
qa.a: At the tea stall by the bus stand.

qa.q: What did Ganga feel when Tushar said her hair looked like a crow's nest with a blank face?
qa.a: She was unsure whether it was a joke, so she answered with her own flat face until his mouth twitched. Only his twitch settled it.

qa.q: What could Ganga do when she cannot tell if Tushar is joking?
qa.a: She can ask him directly, as she did later, and agree when he will signal it.

qa.q: How might the tea seller have seen the exchange?
qa.a: He stopped pouring and shook his head, so he probably wondered if it was an insult or a joke and found it funny only afterwards.

grounding: A teen delivers an insult-like joke without expression, and shared understanding and asking settle the uncertainty.

passage: Abebe stood in the doorway of the youth centre in Addis Ababa and said in a completely flat voice, "Yara, I have decided to become a professional pigeon." Nobody laughed. Yara looked at him, then at the other kids. "Is this a joke?" she asked. Abebe's face stayed perfectly still for four seconds. Then, without blinking, he said, "Yes." Half the room laughed. One boy, Sami, hadn't. He said quietly, "I thought you were sad." Abebe's deadpan cracked. "I'm not. Sorry. I should have said." Yara added, "Some jokes are better with a tiny smile." Abebe said, "Fair," and gave her one, small and crooked.

qa.q: What did Abebe say he had decided to become?
qa.a: A professional pigeon.

qa.q: What was Sami feeling when nobody laughed at Abebe's joke?
qa.a: Sami was unsure and worried, because Abebe's flat face made him think Abebe was sad. Deadpan can hide amusement.

qa.q: What could Abebe do so friends know when he is joking?
qa.a: He can add a small smile or check in when friends look confused.

qa.q: How does Yara see Abebe's deadpan humour?
qa.a: She takes it as a joke but still asks, and she finds a small smile makes it clearer for people who do not know him well.

grounding: A teen delivers a joke deadpan, listeners cannot tell if it is humour, and asking settles it.

passage: Some weeks last term I answered everyone with one word. Fine. Okay. Maybe. I stared at my screen during lunch even when there was nothing on it. My friend Leela kept asking what was wrong, and I kept saying nothing, and honestly it felt true. I was tired, I think, and something had happened at home that I didn't want to explain. Leela did not accuse me of ignoring her. She just sat with me and shared her chips and talked about her cat. After three weeks I said, "Sorry I've been off." She said, "You came back." I told her a little of it then. I'm glad she didn't force it.

qa.q: What did Leela share with the narrator at lunch?
qa.a: Her chips.

qa.q: What was the narrator feeling during the weeks of one-word answers?
qa.a: The narrator was tired and privately hurt by something at home, and not ready to explain. It could also have looked like boredom from the outside.

qa.q: What made Leela's approach helpful?
qa.a: She kept sitting with the narrator, shared food and talked lightly, without accusing or forcing an answer.

qa.q: How might Leela have felt during those weeks?
qa.a: She may have felt worried or shut out, but she stayed patient and let the narrator come back on their own time.

grounding: A teen withdraws with one-word answers for private reasons, and patient check-ins work better than accusations.

passage: Observation note from the youth club, kept by Jeevan. Anirban, 16, arrived late again on Thursday and sat by himself with his phone. Asked if he wanted to join the carrom game, he answered "No" without looking up. In the past fortnight he has said little, and his hair looks uncombed. It would be easy to call him rude or lazy, but I have seen him laugh with the others before. I sat next to him for a while and said nothing about the phone. He said, "Sorry, just tired." I told him he is welcome any time. I have mentioned to his class teacher that he seems low on energy, and I will keep checking in gently.

qa.q: Which game was Anirban asked to join?
qa.a: The carrom game.

qa.q: What might Anirban be feeling, according to Jeevan?
qa.a: He may be tired, since he says so, but the note also leaves open other reasons like hurt or boredom. Jeevan avoids concluding.

qa.q: What did Jeevan do next?
qa.a: He sat with Anirban without commenting on the phone, said he was welcome any time, and told the class teacher he seems low on energy.

qa.q: How might Anirban see Jeevan's approach?
qa.a: He may feel relieved not to be scolded, since being treated as welcome makes it easier to return.

grounding: A teen who withdraws and stares at a screen may be tired, hurt or private, and a patient adult checks in over time.

passage: Dear Arohi, I know you noticed that I didn't react when the results were read out in class yesterday. Everyone else was cheering or groaning, and my face stayed still. Honestly, I got the marks I wanted, but I didn't want the others to see how happy I was, because Renu, who sits behind me, had failed. And earlier this year when I showed hurt over the group photo, some kids made fun of me for it. So now I keep my face blank in front of people. It is easier. It also feels lonely sometimes. Can we talk at the canteen tomorrow? You can pretend not to see my face. Love, Hansa

qa.q: Why does Hansa keep a blank face at school?
qa.a: She wants to avoid showing hurt or joy in front of peers, since she was made fun of for showing hurt earlier.

qa.q: What does Hansa feel about keeping her face blank?
qa.a: She feels it protects her and makes things easier, but it also feels lonely sometimes.

qa.q: What could Arohi do to help Hansa open up?
qa.a: She can offer a relaxed talk in the canteen without pushing, and show she can be trusted.

qa.q: How might Renu see Hansa's blank face?
qa.a: Renu may find it kind or cold, since she cannot tell what lies behind it, and Hansa did it partly for Renu's sake.

grounding: A teen keeps a blank face to avoid showing hurt or joy to peers, which protects privacy but can hide need.

passage: "People say I look like a wall," Zeenat told her cousin Dilnaz, twirling a pen on the recorded call. "At school, anything that shows on my face gets discussed. When Yusuf said my drawing was ugly, I did nothing. I just kept my face still. Same when my drawing won a prize; I wouldn't let them see I was thrilled. But at home with Ammi I let my face out, mostly." Dilnaz said, "I always thought you didn't care." "That's what I want people to think." She stopped twirling the pen. "But I think I want someone to notice anyway." Dilnaz said, "I noticed just now." Zeenat smiled a little, then caught it and let it stay.

qa.q: What did Yusuf say about Zeenat's drawing?
qa.a: He said it was ugly.

qa.q: What does Zeenat feel behind her still face?
qa.a: She feels hurt at the insult and thrilled at the prize, but hides both from peers. She also admits she wants someone to notice.

qa.q: What could Dilnaz do to help Zeenat feel safe showing her feelings?
qa.a: She could keep noticing kindly, leave the door open to talk, and avoid teasing.

qa.q: Why might Dilnaz have thought Zeenat did not care?
qa.a: A blank face gives no clues, so Dilnaz took the stillness as indifference, not protection.

grounding: A teen keeps an impassive face to protect privacy, while hiding both hurt and joy from peers.

subtopic: Visible reactions with multiple possible causes
passage: "Do you know what happens when I get called on?" Pallavi said into the microphone, laughing. "My whole face goes red, like a tomato. It starts at my neck. In class I keep thinking, everybody is looking at my face. Last week I read the school announcement and Uday, who was behind me, said later, 'You looked nervous.' I told him, 'It's just my face.' Afterwards I tried what my cousin said: breathe out slowly, and look at the people, not at what they might think. It helped. Most people were looking at the paper in their hands, not at me. It still went red, but I felt calmer."

qa.q: Where does Pallavi say the redness starts?
qa.a: At her neck.

qa.q: What is Pallavi afraid of when her face goes red?
qa.a: She fears being noticed and judged, and she keeps thinking everyone is looking at her face. Slow breathing and looking outward helped her feel calmer.

qa.q: What could Pallavi try next time she is called on?
qa.a: She could breathe out slowly, look at the people, and remind herself that most are not watching her face.

qa.q: What did Uday see when Pallavi read the announcement?
qa.a: He saw a nervous-looking student, though he could only guess at her feelings, and she did not find out what he thought beyond that.

grounding: A teen who blushes easily fears being noticed, and slow breathing and outward focus reduce the distress.

subtopic: Visible reactions with multiple possible causes
passage: From the second row of the science lab, Indu could see her friend Payal's ears glow pink as their teacher called her name. Payal looked at her page, gripped her pen, and took a slow breath. Indu whispered, "Just read the first line." Payal read it, voice small. By the third line she looked up. By the end her cheeks were still pink, but her voice was steady. Afterwards Indu said, "You went red." "I know," said Payal, laughing. "Nobody said anything though." Indu said, "I didn't even see it until you said." Payal grinned and let out a breath. I think it helps to know how little others notice.

qa.q: What did Indu whisper to Payal?
qa.a: She whispered, "Just read the first line."

qa.q: What might Payal be feeling when her ears turn pink?
qa.a: She is probably anxious about being looked at, but her slow breath and steady voice by the end show it eased. Blushing alone does not tell us how much she is bothered.

qa.q: What helped Payal get through reading aloud?
qa.a: A slow breath, a small first step of one line, and a friend's support.

qa.q: What was Indu's view of Payal's blush?
qa.a: Indu barely noticed it until Payal mentioned it, showing that others often see less than we fear.

grounding: A teen blushes and fears being noticed, and breathing, outward focus and knowing others notice little reduce distress.

subtopic: Visible reactions with multiple possible causes
passage: In the clinic waiting room, the television murmured and a kid coughed. Preeti had come with her friend Vijay for his blood test. When the nurse called his name, Vijay stood, his eyes filling. Preeti thought, He's scared. But she remembered a science-club session where they had talked about tears coming from many causes, so she did not guess. She walked beside him, and said softly, "Do you want to tell me?" He blinked. "It's not the needle. It's that my grandmother used to bring me here." Preeti nodded. "Okay." She stayed beside him in the doorway, and the nurse waited patiently.

qa.q: Who came to the clinic for a blood test?
qa.a: Her friend Vijay had a blood test.

qa.q: Why did Vijay's eyes fill with tears, and what had Preeti first assumed?
qa.a: They were about missing his grandmother, who used to bring him to the clinic, and not about the needle as Preeti first guessed. Tears can come from many causes.

qa.q: What could Preeti do to support Vijay?
qa.a: She could stay beside him, ask gently and accept whatever he shares without pushing.

qa.q: How might the nurse see Vijay's tears?
qa.a: They probably see many kinds of tears and waited patiently, without assuming he was afraid of the needle.

grounding: A teen sees a friend's tears, resists guessing and asks gently, learning they came from something else.

subtopic: Visible reactions with multiple possible causes
passage: Dear Binita, sorry about how I went at your birthday. When you brought out the cake with my face on it, I burst into tears and you looked so worried. I know you thought I was upset. Honestly I was laughing so hard I was crying, and then I remembered how my dad used to make silly cakes, and then I was crying for real. All of it at once. You didn't ask what was wrong, you just held my hand and gave me a napkin, and that helped more than any question. Thank you for staying. Next time I'll say, "It's a good cry." Love, Tenzin

qa.q: What was on the birthday cake?
qa.a: A cake with a face on it, brought out by Binita.

qa.q: What was Tenzin feeling when the tears came?
qa.a: Tenzin was laughing and then remembering the dad who made silly cakes, so joy and sadness mixed. That is why the tears could not be read from outside.

qa.q: What did Binita do that helped?
qa.a: She stayed beside Tenzin, held a hand and offered a napkin without pushing for an explanation.

qa.q: How might Binita have felt when Tenzin burst into tears?
qa.a: She probably felt worried and unsure whether the cake had hurt Tenzin, and relieved by the later explanation.

grounding: A teen reads a friend's tears and learns they came from laughter and sadness together, so staying present beats guessing.
